Designing a Product Catalogue That B2B Buyers Actually Use

B2B buyers use catalogues to compare, specify and justify purchases. A catalogue designed for those jobs becomes a sales tool that keeps working.

VXVintorex Digital team3 min read · Evergreen guide

Key takeaways

  • Organise the catalogue the way buyers search: by application, category or specification.
  • Consistent product pages with clear specs make comparison effortless.
  • Include the information buyers need to get internal approval.
  • Design for both print and digital, including searchable PDFs and web pages.

Understand how buyers use it

B2B buyers rarely read a catalogue cover to cover. They use it to find the right product for an application, compare models, check specifications, share options with colleagues and justify a purchase to their managers. Design every page to make those jobs easy.

Structure

  1. Cover and introduction: who you are, your strengths and certifications in brief.
  2. How to use the catalogue: an index, a product selector chart and a key to symbols.
  3. Product sections: grouped by category or application, colour-coded for quick navigation.
  4. Technical appendix: dimension drawings, performance curves, material data.
  5. Support and contact: service network, warranty, ordering process and contacts.

Product page template

A consistent template lets buyers compare products at a glance.
  • Product name and model number
  • A hero image or render, plus a detail or exploded view
  • Key features and benefits in three to five bullets
  • Typical applications
  • A specification table with consistent units and order across all products
  • Dimension drawing
  • Available variants, options and accessories
  • Certifications and standards

Help the buyer get approval

Purchasing decisions often involve engineers, finance and management. Include information each of them needs: performance data for engineers, efficiency and lifetime cost benefits for finance, and reliability, warranty and support for management. Case studies and client references help too.

Design principles

  • A clean grid and generous white space for readability.
  • Consistent typography and colour coding per section.
  • High-quality, consistent visuals, ideally renders with matching lighting.
  • Tables that are easy to scan, with clear headers and alternating row shading.
  • Brand colours used to guide navigation rather than decorate.

Print and digital

  • Print: correct bleed, colour profiles and resolution, and paper choice suited to frequent handling.
  • Digital PDF: searchable text, clickable table of contents and links, compressed for email.
  • Web: product pages on your website mirroring the catalogue, so search engines and buyers can find individual products.

Keep it current

Plan for updates. Use templates and organised source files so adding products or changing specifications is quick. Put a version number on the catalogue so sales teams know they are sharing the latest edition.

Frequently asked questions

Should prices be in the catalogue?

Usually not in B2B catalogues meant to last, because prices change and vary by customer. Use a separate price list that can be updated independently.

How long should a catalogue be?

Long enough to cover your range clearly. Large ranges may work better as several focused catalogues by category or industry.
